# Affine Transform Pipeline Interpreter (libGDX, Headless)

## Background

Build a command-line interpreter that evaluates named 2D affine-transform pipelines and applies them to points and polygons. The interpreter runs on top of the libGDX game framework (version 1.14.2) using its non-rendering headless backend, so it performs no OpenGL calls and must run fully offline.

## Requirements

* Read a pipeline program from a UTF-8 text file and write results to an output text file.
* Support named pipeline definitions built from the primitive operations `translate`, `rotate`, `scale` and `shear`, plus references to previously-defined pipelines (nested composition).
* Apply named pipelines to points and polygons, reporting the resulting transform matrix, the transformed geometry, the signed area and orientation for polygons, and an inverse round-trip check for probe points.
* The program must run under a libGDX `HeadlessApplication` and terminate by itself.

## Input format

The input file is UTF-8 text, processed line by line. Rules:

* Text from a `#` character to the end of a line is a comment and is ignored. Blank lines are ignored.
* Tokens are separated by arbitrary runs of spaces and/or tabs; leading and trailing whitespace on a line is ignored.
* All keywords are lowercase and case-sensitive. Names match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`. Numbers are decimal values parseable as a Java `float` (optionally signed, with an optional fractional part). All angles are in degrees.

A pipeline definition is:

```
define <name>
  <operation>
  ...
end
```

where each `<operation>` is exactly one of:

* `translate <tx> <ty>`
* `rotate <degrees>`
* `scale <sx> <sy>`
* `shear <shx> <shy>`
* `use <otherName>`

A `use <otherName>` operation may reference only a pipeline whose full `define ... end` block appears earlier in the same file (no forward references, no recursion, no cycles).

Command lines appear only outside of `define ... end` blocks and are one of:

* `point <name> <x> <y>`
* `polygon <name> <x1> <y1> <x2> <y2> ... <xk> <yk>` (k >= 3 vertices, i.e. an even number of at least 6 coordinates)
* `inverse <name> <x> <y>`

## Transform semantics

A 2D affine transform is the 3x3 matrix (with implicit bottom row `0 0 1`) described by six numbers `m00 m01 m02 / m10 m11 m12`. A point `(x, y)` maps to:

```
x' = m00*x + m01*y + m02
y' = m10*x + m11*y + m12
```

The primitive operations denote these matrices:

* `translate tx ty` -> `m00=1 m01=0 m02=tx ; m10=0 m11=1 m12=ty`
* `rotate d` -> counter-clockwise rotation: `m00=cos(d) m01=-sin(d) m02=0 ; m10=sin(d) m11=cos(d) m12=0`
* `scale sx sy` -> `m00=sx m01=0 m02=0 ; m10=0 m11=sy m12=0`
* `shear shx shy` -> `m00=1 m01=shx m02=0 ; m10=shy m11=1 m12=0`

A pipeline evaluates to a matrix `M` as follows: start from the identity matrix; process the pipeline's operations in listed order (top to bottom); each operation `O` updates `M` by post-multiplication `M <- M . O` (the matrix product with the accumulated `M` on the left and the operation's matrix on the right). For a `use <name>` operation, `O` is the fully-evaluated matrix of the referenced pipeline. Consequently the operation listed last is the one applied first to a point.

The determinant is `det = m00*m11 - m01*m10`.

## Output format

Write results to the output file as UTF-8 text with Unix (LF) line endings, one line per command in the same order the commands appear in the input, and a trailing newline after the last line. Every numeric value is formatted with exactly four digits after the decimal point using a period as the decimal separator (US locale). Any value whose four-decimal rendering would be `-0.0000` must instead be written as `0.0000`. Tokens on a line are separated by single spaces.

* For `point <name> <x> <y>`:
  `point <name> matrix <m00> <m01> <m02> <m10> <m11> <m12> image <x'> <y'>`
* For `polygon <name> ...`:
  `polygon <name> matrix <m00> <m01> <m02> <m10> <m11> <m12> area <signedArea> orient <preserved|flipped|degenerate> image <x1'> <y1'> ... <xk'> <yk'>`
  where `<signedArea>` is the signed area of the transformed polygon computed by the shoelace formula over the transformed vertices in listed order, `A = 0.5 * sum over i of (xi'*y(i+1)' - x(i+1)'*yi')` with indices taken modulo k, and `orient` is `preserved` when `det > 0`, `flipped` when `det < 0`, or `degenerate` when `det == 0`.
* For `inverse <name> <x> <y>`: let `p = (x, y)` and `q = M . p`. If `det == 0`, write exactly `inverse <name> matrix <m00> <m01> <m02> <m10> <m11> <m12> singular`. Otherwise let `N = M^-1`, `b = N . q`, and `residual` be the Euclidean distance between `p` and `b`, then write `inverse <name> matrix <m00> <m01> <m02> <m10> <m11> <m12> forward <qx> <qy> back <bx> <by> residual <residual> <ok|fail>`, where the final token is `ok` when `residual <= 1e-3` and `fail` otherwise.

## Implementation Hints

* Project path: /home/user/affine-pipeline
* The project is a preconfigured Gradle project (Gradle 8.10, JDK 17) that already declares the libGDX 1.14.2 core and headless-backend dependencies and applies the `application` plugin with main class `com.example.affine.HeadlessLauncher`; all required dependencies are present in the local Gradle/Maven cache so the project builds and runs offline. Implement that main class and any supporting classes.
* The program receives exactly two arguments, `--input=<path>` and `--output=<path>`; it must read the pipeline program from the input path and write the results to the output path.
* The program must run under a libGDX `HeadlessApplication`, must not perform any graphics or OpenGL calls, and must terminate on its own with exit status 0 after the output file has been fully written.
* It must be runnable from the project path with: `gradle --offline run --args="--input=<inputPath> --output=<outputPath>"`.
I'll start by looking at how the project is organized.

I'm setting up the project structure with a headless launcher that will handle command-line argument parsing and run the interpreter through a simple ApplicationListener. The main flow will execute all processing in the create() method, output results, then exit cleanly. I'm planning core classes like a Matrix type for the affine transformations.

Now I'm working through the parsing logic: tokenization strips comments and whitespace, then I'll maintain a map of named pipelines. The interpreter processes lines sequentially—skipping empty ones, handling "define" blocks that build matrices by composing operations in order starting from identity, and executing other commands like point, patch, and polygon operations that reference previously defined pipelines.

For the matrix math, I need to implement affine matrix multiplication where two 3x3 matrices compose with the implicit bottom row [0 0 1], so the result combines the transformation components correctly. Then point transformation applies the final matrix to coordinates.

For the inverse, I'm computing the determinant of the 2x2 linear part, then using the standard formula to invert the affine matrix—the inverse of the linear part gets scaled by 1/det, and the translation component gets adjusted accordingly so that multiplying the inverse by the original gives the identity.

For number formatting, I'm using Java's String.format with US locale to get exactly 4 decimal places, then handling the edge case where negative zero appears by replacing "-0.0000" with "0.0000".

Now I'm setting up the main application class that extends ApplicationAdapter, where the create() method will run the interpreter, write the output file, and exit the application—making sure to handle exceptions properly so the app terminates cleanly.

For the HeadlessLauncher, I need to parse the --input and --output command-line arguments, set up a HeadlessApplicationConfiguration, and instantiate HeadlessApplication with the listener. The tricky part is that the headless app normally loops through render() calls, but I want it to execute once and exit immediately after create() finishes.

My approach is to do all the processing inside the create() method and then call Gdx.app.exit() to cleanly stop the render loop. I'm checking whether Gdx.app.exit() is reliable enough or if I should use System.exit() instead, since the HeadlessApplication runs its own thread loop and exit() just sets a flag to stop it. I'll handle the threading issue by doing all the work synchronously inside the create() method, then calling System.exit(0) directly once the output is written—that way the process terminates immediately after completion regardless of how HeadlessApplication manages its threads.

Now I'm structuring the code across multiple files: a main launcher class to handle argument parsing and instantiate HeadlessApplication, an ApplicationAdapter subclass that performs the actual matrix operations and pipeline interpretation, a matrix class for the affine transformations, and an interpreter class for parsing and executing the pipeline commands.

For number formatting, I need to handle Java's float precision by converting to double and formatting to four decimal places using the US locale, plus checking for negative zero in the formatted output. The input parsing uses a state machine approach where normal mode processes commands directly, and when encountering a "define" block, I collect all operations until reaching an "end" marker, then build the operation list and compute the resulting transformation matrix.

For the "point" command, I look up the pipeline's transformation matrix, apply it to the input coordinates, and output the result. The "polygon" command transforms all vertices, calculates the area using the shoelace formula, and determines orientation from the determinant sign. The "inverse" command computes the forward transformation, checks if the matrix is singular, and if not, applies the inverse matrix to get the original point, then calculates the residual error.

Writing the Java implementation...
I need to set up the source directory and create the initial files.
Now I'm working on the PipelineInterpreter class to handle parsing the pipeline configuration, executing the stages, and managing the output generation.
Now the HeadlessLauncher and ApplicationListener classes:
I should verify the gradle setup by checking if the wrapper exists and whether gradle is available on the system.

Implemented the affine transform pipeline interpreter at `/home/user/affine-pipeline`:

- `src/main/java/com/example/affine/AffineMatrix.java` — 2D affine matrix (m00,m01,m02,m10,m11,m12) with `translate`/`rotate`/`scale`/`shear` factory methods, post-multiplication (`this . other`), determinant, point application, and inverse computation.
- `src/main/java/com/example/affine/PipelineInterpreter.java` — parses the UTF-8 input file line by line (stripping `#` comments and blank lines, tokenizing on runs of spaces/tabs), handles `define ... end` blocks (building each pipeline's matrix via sequential post-multiplication, including `use` references to earlier-defined pipelines), and executes `point`/`polygon`/`inverse` commands, producing output lines exactly per the spec (4-decimal formatting via `%.4f` in `Locale.US`, with `-0.0000` normalized to `0.0000`; shoelace area; `preserved/flipped/degenerate` orientation from `det`; singular/forward/back/residual/ok-fail logic for `inverse`). Output is written as UTF-8 with LF endings and a trailing newline.
- `src/main/java/com/example/affine/AffineApplicationListener.java` — `ApplicationAdapter` that runs the interpreter synchronously inside `create()` (no GL calls) and calls `System.exit(...)` once the output file is fully written, guaranteeing the process terminates on its own.
- `src/main/java/com/example/affine/HeadlessLauncher.java` — the declared main class; parses `--input=` and `--output=` args and boots a `HeadlessApplication` with `HeadlessApplicationConfiguration`.

Verified with `gradle --offline run --args="--input=<in> --output=<out>"` using hand-checked sample pipelines (nested `use` composition, translate+rotate+scale, singular scale-by-zero pipeline): matrices, transformed points/polygons, signed area/orientation, and inverse round-trip/residual all compute correctly, negative-zero values are normalized to `0.0000`, the output file uses LF line endings with a trailing newline, and the Gradle `run` task completes with exit code 0 in under 2 seconds.
